Flood JL and Dodgson JE conducted a study in 2010 that explored healthcare and social service providers' observations and descriptions of breastfeeding patterns among Pacific Islander mothers. This research was published in the Journal of Midwifery & Women’s Health. 2. Bergh AM, in a 1993 study published in Curationis, identified both obstacles to and motivations for successful breastfeeding, providing insights into factors that influence breastfeeding practices. 3. Furber CM and Thomson AM, in a 2008 qualitative study published in the International Journal of Nursing Studies, examined the emotional experiences of English midwives as they integrated breastfeeding knowledge into their clinical practice. 4. Nelson AM, in a 2007 study published in the Journal of Advanced Nursing, investigated the experiences of maternal-newborn nurses regarding inconsistent professional support for breastfeeding, highlighting challenges in providing uniform care. 5. Becker GE, in a 1992 study published in the Journal of Human Lactation, assessed the breastfeeding knowledge of hospital staff working in rural maternity units in Ireland, identifying gaps in education and training. 6. Karnawat BS, Singh RN, Gupta BD, and Chaudhury SP, in a 1987 study published in Indian Pediatrics, evaluated the knowledge and attitudes of hospital employees regarding infant feeding practices, emphasizing the need for improved awareness and education. 7. Ouyang YQ, Xu YX, and Zhang Q conducted a 2012 survey published in Nursing & Health Sciences, which examined breastfeeding practices among Chinese female physicians and nurses, shedding light on their personal and professional experiences. 8. Lazzaro E, Anderson J, and Auld G, in a 1995 study published in the Journal of Human Lactation, explored the attitudes of medical professionals toward breastfeeding, identifying factors that influence their support for breastfeeding mothers. 9. Freed GL, Clark SJ, Lohr JA, and Sorenson JR, in a 1995 national study published in Pediatrics, analyzed the involvement of pediatricians in breastfeeding promotion, focusing on the practices of both residents and practitioners. 10. Freed GL, Jones TM, and Fraley JK, in a 1992 study published in the Southern Medical Journal, investigated the attitudes and education of pediatric house staff regarding breastfeeding, highlighting the need for enhanced training. 11. Haager-Bürkert H, Niebuhr D, and Kroke A, in a 2010 study published in Geburtshilfe Frauenheilkunde, examined the perceived challenges faced by German maternity clinics in obtaining Baby-Friendly Hospital certification. 12. Szucs KA, Miracle DJ, and Rosenman MB, in a 2009 study published in Breastfeeding Medicine, assessed the breastfeeding knowledge, attitudes, and practices of healthcare providers working in a medical home setting. 13. Ward KN and Byrne JP, in a 2011 critical review published in the Journal of Human Lactation, evaluated the impact of continuing breastfeeding education provided to nurses and midwives, emphasizing the importance of ongoing professional development. 14. Furber CM and Thomson AM, in a 2006 study published in Midwifery, explored deviations from standard baby-feeding practices in the UK, discussing both instances of non-compliance and examples of good practice. 15. Moore T, Gauld R, and Williams S, in a 2007 study published in the International Breastfeeding Journal, analyzed the implementation of Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative policies in New Zealand public hospitals. 16. Cantrill RM, Creedy DK, and Cooke M, in a 2003 Australian study published in Midwifery, assessed the breastfeeding knowledge of midwives, identifying areas for improvement in their education and training. 17. Ekström A, Matthiesen AS, Widström AM, and Nissen E, in a 2005 study published in the Scandinavian Journal of Public Health, examined the attitudes of health professionals who provide breastfeeding counseling, highlighting their role in supporting mothers. 18. Ellis DJ and Hewat RJ, in a 1983 study published in the Journal of Advanced Nursing, investigated whether nurses help or hinder mothers who breastfeed, providing insights into the impact of nursing practices on breastfeeding success. 19. Hellings P and Howe C, in a 2000 study published in the Journal of Midwifery & Women’s Health, assessed the breastfeeding knowledge of nurse practitioners and nurse-midwives, emphasizing the need for comprehensive training. 20. Krogstrand KS and Parr K, in a 2005 study published in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association, reported that physicians requested more problem-solving information to better promote and support breastfeeding. 21. Goldstein AO and Freed GL, in a 1992 study published in Family Medicine, examined the breastfeeding counseling practices of family practice residents, identifying areas for improvement in their training. 22. Minnie CS and Greeff M, in a 2006 study published in Curationis, explored the decision-making process of mothers regarding infant feeding in the context of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, discussing the implications for health education. 23. Tennant R, Wallace LM, and Law S, in a 2006 qualitative study published in Community Practice, identified barriers to breastfeeding from the perspectives of health professionals and lay counselors. 24. Garner CD, Ratcliff SL, Thornburg LL, Wethington E, Howard CR, and Rasmussen KM, in a 2016 study published in Breastfeeding Medicine, highlighted the discontinuity of breastfeeding care, describing it as a lack of coordinated support. 25. Anchondo I, Berkeley L, Mulla ZD, Byrd T, Nuwayhid B, Handal G, et al., in a 2012 commentary published in the Southern Medical Journal, discussed the experiences and attitudes of pediatricians, obstetricians, gynecologists, and family medicine physicians regarding breastfeeding. 26. Taveras EM, Li R, Grummer-Strawn L, Richardson M, Marshall R, Rêgo VH, et al., in a 2004 study published in Pediatrics, analyzed the opinions and practices of clinicians associated with the continuation of exclusive breastfeeding. 27. Wallace LM and Kosmala-Anderson J, in a 2006 survey published in Maternal & Child Nutrition, assessed the training needs of doctors in England regarding breastfeeding support skills. 28. Guidelines emphasize the importance of early skin-to-skin contact between mothers and infants immediately after birth to increase the rates of early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour. 29. Guidelines recommend assisting mothers with correct positioning and attachment during breastfeeding to ensure effective infant suckling and improve exclusive breastfeeding rates. 30. Guidelines discourage the use of pacifiers or artificial teats for breastfed infants to promote exclusive breastfeeding and reduce potential interference with breastfeeding practices. 31. Guidelines advocate for rooming-in practices, where mothers and infants remain together during their hospital stay, to support exclusive breastfeeding and strengthen maternal-infant bonding. 32. Guidelines recommend feeding infants on demand rather than on a schedule to enhance exclusive breastfeeding rates and support infant-led feeding cues. 33. Guidelines advise against providing newborns with additional foods or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated, to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 34. Guidelines emphasize the importance of having a written breastfeeding policy in maternity and newborn care facilities, which is routinely communicated to staff, to support early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding. 35. Guidelines highlight the need for comprehensive training of healthcare workers in breastfeeding support to ensure consistent and effective care for breastfeeding mothers and their infants.
